title.narrative: NIHR HPSR-CA - Preventing blindness in children by integrating eye health into child health policies and systems

description.narrative:
Many young children in lower- and middle-income countries (LMICs) become or remain blind because of a lack of eye care at the primary level of care. This means that some eye conditions are not being prevented, and children with treatable conditions are not being detected and treated early. We are addressing this by strengthening the health system at the primary level in Tanzania and Nepal.
Our health system model has the following components: including eye care in the training materials of staff at the primary level who deliver the World Health Organization's (WHO) program, the Integrated Management of Newborn and Childhood Illness; improving staff supervision; providing staff with a device to test children’s eyes (Arclight); improving the referral of children who need to be seen by an eye specialist; adding eye conditions in the system staff use to document the conditions detected in children who attend the health facility, and improving awareness of the need for an eye test by including this in the booklet for parents.
The project will start in November 2024 and run for five years. There will be five inter-connected studies:
1. Collecting baseline information on what is already in place in primary health facilities and whether there are other gaps to address in our model. 2. A randomised trial in which all the components outlined above will be rolled out at intervals in a randomised manner in selected districts. We will assess whether more children are identified with eye or vision problems and receive appropriate care after the elements have been rolled out compared with before. 3. Alongside the trial we will collect information from a range of different sources to find out what is working well, for whom and how (i.e., a process evaluation). 4. An analysis of the costs and effectiveness of the model using data from the trial. 5. A study to understand factors which might enable or hinder subsequent scaling-up of the model.
Community engagement activities will take place throughout the project. The project is being led by the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, UK and Kilimanjaro Christian Medical College in Tanzania. The other partners are Muhibilli University Hospital and Allied Sciences in Tanzania, and Nepal Netra Jyoti Sangh and Kathmandu Medical College in Nepal. In each country the Ministry of Health and WHO representatives are actively involved.

The project has 5 objectives:
1.In selected districts in Nepal and Tanzania we will collect information from primary level facility records, staff and parents, and districts supervisors and managers. We will also review relevant policy documents. The data will be analysed to find out whether the health systems strengthening model we have developed needs to be modified, and will provide baseline data for objectives 3 and 4. 2. The districts will be randomly allocated to different time periods when the health system strengthening model will be delivered to health facilities within the district. There will be four training phases and the trial will last 35 months. Data will be collected over 35 months from health facilities and referral hospitals. 3. During the trial, data will be collected from multiple sources to assess: how the intervention was implemented, the context of implementation and how the interventions brought about change. Findings will be used to recommend alterations to the model to be considered for scale up to other countries. 4. Data on the additional costs of delivering the health system strengthening model will be obtained from multiple sources (e.g., training costs). Data from the trial will provide measures of effectiveness. 5. Interviews will be conducted with key individuals in each country, regionally and globally to seek their views on scaling up the health systems strengthening model.
